name: King's Gambit
subtitle: Trade a pawn for the initiative.

ideas.idea: Offer the f-pawn to pull Black's central pawn away from the centre. Your compensation is time: build a broad centre, develop with threats, and make the open f-file useful before Black can consolidate. The sacrifice is a practical invitation to an unbalanced fight, not a promise of an advantage.
ideas.structure: The e- and d-pawns can claim central space, but advancing them carelessly leaves squares behind. Black's extra pawn on the f-file can restrict your pieces or become a target. If Black supports it with king-side pawns, look at the squares those pawns have stopped defending before deciding to break the chain.
ideas.pieces: A knight often belongs on f3, both developing and reducing checks on the queen's diagonal. The light-squared bishop looks toward f7, and castling can bring a rook to the open file. Finish mobilizing your queen-side pieces rather than expecting two attackers to do all the work.
ideas.motifs: Watch the diagonal leading to h4: moving the f-pawn has weakened your own king. Pressure on f7, discoveries along the f-file, and attacks on a stretched pawn chain are recurring themes. A flashy sacrifice on f7 needs a concrete calculation, not just a familiar pattern.
ideas.declined: If Black develops a bishop instead of taking, claim the centre without assuming you have won a free tempo. A central counterstrike asks a different question: resolve the central tension and watch for an advanced enemy e-pawn that can gain time against your pieces.
ideas.caution: Your king is part of the price. If the attack stalls, stop chasing the pawn and improve king safety. Black can defend accurately and retain a sound position.
